etymology: Hebrew Anim, perhaps “springs” or “fountains” (a dual form of ayin, spring); a town in the hill country of Judah near Eshtemoh, named once.
biblical_def: Anim was a town in the hill country of Judah, in the district that reached toward Debir and Eshtemoh, listed once: “And Anab, and Eshtemoh, and Anim” (Josh 15:50). If the name means “springs,” it marks a place of water in the highlands, and water in that dry land was life and blessing. The hill country of Judah was Caleb’s country, the region of Hebron, given to the man who wholly followed the LORD; and every town in it was part of the inheritance sworn to Israel. Anim, a small spring-town among the hills, joins the witness of all these places to the goodness and fidelity of God, who “gave for an inheritance” the whole land He had promised. The springs of Anim also whisper of the deeper thirst that no earthly water can slake, and of the LORD who is the fountain of living waters, whom His people forsake at their peril. He that drinketh of the water Christ gives shall never thirst, but it shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life. Anim, a fountain in the hills of Judah, is a small sign pointing to that unfailing spring.
webster_summary: A town in the hill country of Judah, perhaps “springs” (Josh 15:50); a sign pointing to the LORD, the fountain of living waters.

The principle to recover is that God is the fountain of living waters. Israel’s great sin was to forsake that fountain and hew out broken cisterns that could hold no water. The springs of an obscure hill-town preach the same gospel the Lord preached at Jacob’s well: the water of this world leaves a man thirsting again, but the water Christ gives becomes in him a well springing up unto everlasting life.

etymology: Hebrew Yoqdeam, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “burning of the people”; a town in the hill country of Judah, named once.
biblical_def: Jokdeam was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed once between Jezreel and Zanoah: “And Jezreel, and Jokdeam, and Zanoah” (Josh 15:56). It lay in the highland district of Judah, in the same country as Maon and Carmel and Ziph, the wilderness where David hid from Saul and where Nabal fed his flocks. Nothing of Jokdeam’s particular history is told; it is a name and no more. Yet these obscure hill-towns together make up the inheritance of Judah, the royal tribe from which the Lion of the tribe of Judah would come. The whole roll of them is sealed with the words, “This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their families” (Josh 15:20). Jokdeam preaches, with all its silent neighbours, that God keeps a record of what men forget. The town whose deeds are lost to history is not lost to God, who numbers the hairs of the head and writes the names of His people in the Lamb’s book of life. The obscurity of Jokdeam is a comfort to every hidden and forgotten saint: the LORD forgets nothing that is His.

etymology: Hebrew Beth Anoth, perhaps “house of answers” or “house of Anath” (a Canaanite goddess); a town in the hill country of Judah, named once.
biblical_def: Beth-anoth was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed once in a group of six cities: “And Maarath, and Bethanoth, and Eltekon; six cities with their villages” (Josh 15:59). Its name may echo Anath, a Canaanite goddess, a reminder that Israel took possession of a land whose very towns were named for false deities; or it may mean “house of answers,” a place where God’s people sought and found response from heaven. Either way the town preaches the great work of the conquest: the LORD gave His people a land steeped in idolatry, that they might purge it and turn its very stones to His glory. The names of the old gods survived in the soil, but the worship of them was to be rooted out; where a Beth-anath had been a house of Anath, it was now to be a place where the true God alone was sought. Israel was called to be a holy people in an unholy land, distinct and separate, keeping herself from idols. Beth-anoth in the hills is a small witness to that calling, and a warning that a people may possess the outward land yet perish if they do not cast the idols out of the heart.

The principle to recover is separation from idols. Israel was given a land whose towns bore the names of false gods, and she was to root out that worship utterly, keeping herself unspotted from the idolatry around her. The apostle’s last word to the church is the same: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols.” A people may hold the outward land and yet perish, if the idol keeps its throne in the heart.

etymology: Hebrew Chumtah, perhaps “place of lizards” or “fortress”; a town in the hill country of Judah near Hebron, named once.
biblical_def: Humtah was a town in the hill country of Judah, named once and set immediately before the greatest city of that region: “And Humtah, and Kirjatharba, which is Hebron, and Zior; nine cities with their villages” (Josh 15:54). Its neighbour was Hebron, the ancient city where Abraham pitched his tent by the oaks of Mamre, where the patriarchs and their wives were buried in the cave of Machpelah, and which Caleb received for his inheritance because he wholly followed the LORD. Humtah, obscure and unremembered, stood in the shadow of that great and holy place. The town preaches the honour of nearness to what God has blessed. As Humtah lay hard by Hebron, the city of the patriarchs and of Caleb’s faith, so the humblest believer is set near the great things of God, a fellow-citizen with the saints and of the household of God. There are no obscure members in the body of Christ; the town next to Hebron shares in Hebron’s glory. Humtah reminds every unremarkable saint that to dwell near the promises, in the fellowship of the faithful, is honour enough, though the world never learn one’s name.

etymology: Hebrew Chetsron, “enclosure” or “courtyard”; a place on the southern border of Judah, near Kadesh-barnea and Addar; distinct from Hezron the son of Pharez.
biblical_def: Hezron was a place on the southern boundary of the tribe of Judah, named in the tracing of the border toward Edom: “And it went out to the south side to Maalehacrabbim, and passed along to Zin, and ascended up on the south side unto Kadeshbarnea, and passed along to Hezron, and went up to Adar” (Josh 15:3). This is a place, not the patriarch Hezron the son of Pharez of Judah, though the two share a name. The word means an enclosure or courtyard, a settled and bounded place in the open desert. Its office in Scripture is to mark a line: the border of the promised inheritance ran through it. The setting of borders is a work of God, for “the most High divided to the nations their inheritance” and “set the bounds of the people” (Deu 32:8). Hezron on the border preaches the wisdom and kindness of a God who appoints bounds, who says to the sea and to the nations, hitherto shalt thou come and no further. The believer, too, has his bounds set by a loving hand; the lines are fallen unto him in pleasant places, and he learns to rest content within the enclosure God has drawn, trusting the Surveyor of all the earth to do right.
webster_summary: A place on the southern border of Judah near Kadesh-barnea (Josh 15:3), distinct from the patriarch Hezron; a witness that God appoints the bounds of His people’s habitation.

etymology: Hebrew Eder, “flock” or “fold”; a town in the far south of Judah toward the border of Edom, named once; distinct from the tower of Edar near Bethlehem.
biblical_def: Eder was a town among the uttermost cities of Judah toward the coast of Edom, listed at the head of that southern roll: “And the uttermost cities of the tribe of the children of Judah toward the coast of Edom southward were Kabzeel, and Eder, and Jagur” (Josh 15:21). The name means “flock” or “fold,” fitting for a town in the great grazing lands of the south, where flocks and herds were the wealth of the people. This town is distinct from the tower of Edar near Bethlehem where Jacob spread his tent. A fold on the frontier is a homely and fitting picture of the people of God, who are His flock, the sheep of His pasture. The LORD is the Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock; and the Lord Jesus is the good Shepherd who gives His life for the sheep and gathers them into one fold. Eder, a sheepfold-town on the edge of the wilderness, preaches the tender care of the Shepherd who seeks the straying, binds up the broken, and will bring all His scattered flock at last into the fold where there shall be one flock and one Shepherd.

etymology: Hebrew Maaleh Aqrabbim, “the ascent of scorpions” (also the ascent of Akrabbim); a steep pass on the southern border of Judah and of the promised land.
biblical_def: Maaleh-acrabbim, “the ascent of scorpions,” was a steep and rugged pass marking the southern border of Judah and of the whole land: “And it went out to the south side to Maalehacrabbim, and passed along to Zin” (Josh 15:3); and again in the tracing of the national boundary, “your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim” (Num 34:4). It was a hard climb through country infested with scorpions, a fitting emblem of the toil and danger by which the border of the promise was reached. The wilderness through which Israel passed was “that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions,” and yet the LORD led His people through it and brought them up. The ascent of scorpions preaches that the way into the inheritance is upward and beset with dangers, but that God is faithful to bring His people through. So the Christian’s path to the heavenly Canaan is steep and thronged with enemies, yet the Lord has given His own authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall by any means hurt them. The scorpion-pass is climbed, and the promised land lies beyond.

etymology: Hebrew Middin, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “measures” or “judgment”; one of the six cities in the wilderness of Judah, near the Dead Sea, named once.
biblical_def: Middin was one of six towns in the wilderness of Judah, the desolate country falling toward the Salt Sea, listed with Beth-arabah and Secacah: “In the wilderness, Betharabah, Middin, and Secacah” (Josh 15:61). It lay in the barren, broken land above the Dead Sea, a place of few and hardy inhabitants. That the inheritance of Judah reached even into that forbidding wilderness is a striking testimony: the LORD gave His people not only the pleasant valleys and fruitful hills but the hard desert places too, and He set families to dwell there. The wilderness towns preach that God is present and provident even in the waste and howling places. It was in the wilderness of Judah that David was hunted and hidden, that John the Baptist cried in preparation for the Lord, and that the Lord Jesus was led up to be tempted and there overcame. The desert is not outside the care of God; He can spread a table in the wilderness and make the parched ground a pool. Middin, a town in that lonely country, witnesses that no place is too barren for the presence and provision of the God of the whole earth.

etymology: Hebrew Ir ha-Melach, “the city of Salt”; one of the six wilderness cities of Judah, near the Salt Sea and En-gedi, named once.
biblical_def: The City of Salt was one of the six towns in the wilderness of Judah, set near the Salt Sea and En-gedi: “And Nibshan, and the city of Salt, and Engedi; six cities with their villages” (Josh 15:62). It took its name from the salt country about the Dead Sea, where the waters are bitter and the very ground is crusted with salt, and where Lot’s wife became a pillar of salt looking back on the doomed cities of the plain. Salt in Scripture is a two-edged emblem. It is the sign of barrenness and curse, for a land overthrown is sown with salt and made a perpetual desolation; yet it is also the sign of covenant and preservation, for every meat-offering was seasoned with the salt of the covenant, and the Lord Jesus called His people the salt of the earth. The City of Salt in the wilderness holds both meanings before the eye: the barren salt of judgment on the cities of the plain, and the savoury salt of the covenant that keeps from corruption. The believer is called to be salt indeed — to have salt in himself, to be at peace, and to season the world with grace — lest, having lost his savour, he be good for nothing but to be cast out.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A town named once in the salt wilderness raises no modern quarrel. Its name simply opens the rich biblical symbol of salt, which cuts two ways: judgment and covenant, barrenness and preservation.

The principle to recover is the double savour of salt. The salt country witnesses the curse on the cities of the plain, where Lot’s wife became a pillar of salt; yet salt is also the sign of the covenant, wherewith every offering was seasoned, and the emblem of the disciple who preserves the world from corruption. “Ye are the salt of the earth,” said the Lord; let the believer keep his savour, have salt in himself, and be at peace.

etymology: Hebrew Migdal Eder, “the tower of the flock” (the tower of Edar); a watchtower and place near Bethlehem where Jacob pitched his tent after Rachel’s death.
biblical_def: Migdal-eder, “the tower of the flock,” was a place near Bethlehem, first named when Jacob, having buried Rachel in the way to Ephrath, journeyed on: “And Israel journeyed, and spread his tent beyond the tower of Edar” (Gen 35:21). It was a shepherds’ watchtower over the fields where the flocks of Bethlehem grazed — the same fields where, in the fulness of time, “there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night” (Luk 2:8), to whom the angel proclaimed the Saviour born in the city of David. The prophet Micah lifts the name to its height: “And thou, O tower of the flock, the strong hold of the daughter of Zion, unto thee shall it come, even the first dominion; the kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem” (Mic 4:8). The tower of the flock thus binds together Rachel’s grave, the shepherd-fields of Bethlehem, and the coming of the King. The good Shepherd was born where the shepherds watched their flocks, hard by the tower of the flock; and the first dominion, lost in Eden, comes at last to Zion through Him. Migdal-eder is a small place freighted with great glory, watching over the fields where the Lamb of God was laid.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A shepherds’ tower near Bethlehem raises no modern quarrel. Its glory is in its associations: Rachel’s grave nearby, the flocks of Bethlehem, and the prophecy of Micah that makes it the strong hold of the daughter of Zion.

The principle to recover is that God gathered the great things of redemption around this small place. The good Shepherd was born where shepherds watched their flocks near the tower of the flock; and Micah declares that to it “shall come the first dominion” (Mic 4:8), the kingdom restored to Zion through the coming King. Bethlehem’s tower of the flock watches still, in the memory of Scripture, over the fields where the Lamb of God was laid in a manger.
